iac-ansible.md:
## Why it exists
Terraform can create a virtual machine. Something still has to make that machine useful: install packages, create users, write config files, harden SSH, start services, rotate a certificate. Doing that by hand over SSH produces **snowflake servers** that nobody can rebuild. **Configuration management** describes the desired state of a machine in versioned files and a tool converges the machine to it, again and again, safely.

Ansible is the most widely used tool for this. It is **agentless**: the control node connects to managed nodes over SSH (WinRM or similar for Windows), runs small modules, and removes them. The language is YAML, the model is push, and the key property is **idempotency**: running the same playbook twice changes nothing the second time.

{{dg:0}}

## Core vocabulary
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Control node** | The machine where you run `ansible-playbook` (needs Python; Linux or macOS, WSL on Windows) |
| **Managed node** | A target host; usually needs only SSH and Python |
| **Inventory** | Which hosts exist and how they are grouped |
| **Module** | A unit of work (`package`, `template`, `service`, `user`), idempotent where it can be |
| **Task** | One module call with arguments |
| **Play and playbook** | A play maps a host group to tasks and roles; a playbook is a list of plays |
| **Role** | A reusable folder layout bundling tasks, defaults, templates, handlers and files |
| **Collection** | A distributable package of modules, plugins and roles (`ansible.posix`, `amazon.aws`, `community.general`) |
| **Facts** | Data gathered from the host (OS family, IPs, memory) |
| **Handler** | A task that runs only when notified by a task that changed something |
| **Vault** | Built-in encryption for secret variables and files |

## Worked example: a project you can copy
```
site.yml
ansible.cfg
requirements.yml
inventory/
  hosts.yml
  group_vars/
    all.yml
    web.yml
roles/
  nginx/
    defaults/main.yml
    tasks/main.yml
    handlers/main.yml
    templates/site.conf.j2
```

`inventory/hosts.yml`:
```yaml
all:
  children:
    web:
      hosts:
        web1.example.com:
        web2.example.com:
    db:
      hosts:
        db1.example.com:
  vars:
    ansible_user: deploy
```

`site.yml`:
```yaml
- name: Configure the web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  serial: "50%"          # roll through half the hosts at a time
  roles:
    - role: nginx
      vars:
        nginx_server_name: shop.example.com
```

`roles/nginx/defaults/main.yml`:
```yaml
nginx_server_name: example.com
nginx_listen_port: 80
```

`roles/nginx/tasks/main.yml`:
```yaml
- name: Install nginx
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: nginx
    state: present

- name: Render the site config
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: site.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/site.conf
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: "0644"
  notify: Reload nginx

- name: Enable and start nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: started
    enabled: true
```

`roles/nginx/handlers/main.yml`:
```yaml
- name: Reload nginx
  ansible.builtin.service:
    name: nginx
    state: reloaded
```

`roles/nginx/templates/site.conf.j2`:
```
server {
    listen {{ nginx_listen_port }};
    server_name {{ nginx_server_name }};
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080;
    }
}
```

Run it safely:
```bash
ansible-inventory -i inventory/hosts.yml --graph              # does the inventory look right?
ansible all -i inventory/hosts.yml -m ansible.builtin.ping    # can we reach everything?
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml site.yml --check --diff   # preview, change nothing
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml site.yml --limit web1.example.com   # one canary host
ansible-playbook -i inventory/hosts.yml site.yml              # everything; a second run should show changed=0
```

## Idempotency is your job when you use `command` or `shell`
Dedicated modules know how to check state. `command` and `shell` do not, so you tell Ansible when the work is already done.

```yaml
- name: Initialise the app database once
  ansible.builtin.command: /opt/app/bin/init-db
  args:
    creates: /var/lib/app/.db-initialised

- name: Report pending migrations without marking the host changed
  ansible.builtin.command: /opt/app/bin/migrate --dry-run
  register: dry
  changed_when: false
  check_mode: false
```
If a second run reports `changed` for something that did not really change, fix it: the noise hides real drift.

## Validating risky files before they land
```yaml
- name: Harden sshd
  ansible.builtin.template:
    src: sshd_config.j2
    dest: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
    owner: root
    group: root
    mode: "0600"
    validate: /usr/sbin/sshd -t -f %s     # refuses to install a config sshd rejects
  notify: Restart sshd
```
A `validate` command stops you from locking yourself out with a broken config.

## Inventories, from static to dynamic
Static files are fine for a handful of hosts. In cloud environments hosts come and go, so use an **inventory plugin**:

```yaml
# inventory/aws_ec2.yml  (the file name must end in aws_ec2.yml)
plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2
regions:
  - eu-west-1
filters:
  tag:Environment: prod
keyed_groups:
  - key: tags.Role
    prefix: role
```
Hosts tagged `Role=web` land in the group `role_web`. Azure has an equivalent plugin in the `azure.azcollection` collection. Tag your infrastructure in Terraform and let Ansible read the tags, so there is no hand-maintained host list.

## Collections and fully qualified names
Always write `ansible.builtin.copy`, not `copy`. Fully qualified collection names (FQCN) make it unambiguous where a module comes from and survive collection changes.

```yaml
# requirements.yml
collections:
  - name: ansible.posix
  - name: community.general
  - name: amazon.aws
```
```bash
ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml
```
Pin versions in `requirements.yml` and install in CI so builds are repeatable.

## Variables, facts and precedence
Ansible has many places a variable can come from (role defaults, inventory, group_vars, host_vars, play vars, `-e` extra vars). Extra vars win; role `defaults/` are the weakest on purpose, so users can override them. Keep it simple:
- Put safe defaults in `roles/<name>/defaults/main.yml`.
- Put environment differences in `inventory/group_vars/<group>.yml`.
- Avoid setting the same variable in four places.

Prefer the dictionary form of facts, `ansible_facts['distribution']`, over the injected short names such as `ansible_distribution`. The short names are on a deprecation path (see the version note).

```yaml
- name: Install the web server package by OS family
  ansible.builtin.package:
    name: "{{ 'apache2' if ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'Debian' else 'httpd' }}"
    state: present
```

## Secrets
```bash
ansible-vault create inventory/group_vars/all/vault.yml
ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cret' --name 'vault_db_password'
ansible-playbook site.yml --vault-id prod@prompt
```
Pattern: keep `db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}"` in a readable file and the encrypted value in the vault file, so searches still find the variable name. For anything shared, prefer a **lookup** against a real secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager via `amazon.aws`, HashiCorp Vault via `community.hashi_vault`) so the secret never sits in Git. Add `no_log: true` to tasks that handle secrets so they do not print in logs.

## Testing and linting
| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| `ansible-lint` | Style and correctness rules (FQCN, risky shell use, missing `name`) |
| `--syntax-check` and `--check --diff` | Parse and preview |
| **Molecule** | Spin up a throwaway container or VM, run the role (converge), run it again to prove idempotence, then run verification tests |
| Testinfra or Ansible assertions | Verify the end state (port open, file present) |

A healthy CI job runs `ansible-lint`, then Molecule on the role, then a `--check` against staging. Molecule's default driver is `delegated`, and it does not bundle `ansible-lint`; for throwaway containers install a driver package (`pip install molecule "molecule-plugins[docker]" ansible-lint`, plus `ansible-galaxy collection install community.docker`) or use the `ansible-dev-tools` package, which bundles the usual tools.

## Running at scale
- **Forks** (default 5) set how many hosts run in parallel; raise it for large fleets.
- **SSH pipelining** and connection multiplexing (ControlPersist) cut per-task overhead.
- **`serial`** limits how many hosts change at once; **`max_fail_percentage`** stops a bad change early.
- **`async` and `poll`** run long tasks without holding the connection.
- **Fact caching** and `gather_facts: false` where you do not need facts speed up big runs.
- **AWX** (the upstream project) and Red Hat Ansible Automation Platform add a web UI, RBAC, scheduling, credentials and job history around the same playbooks.
- **`ansible-pull`** inverts the model: hosts fetch the playbook from Git and apply it locally.

## Ansible, Terraform, Packer and GitOps: who does what
| Tool | Good at | Not for |
|---|---|---|
| **Terraform / OpenTofu** | Creating and wiring cloud resources, tracking them in state | Fine-grained in-OS configuration |
| **Ansible** | Configuring OS, packages, files, services, one-off orchestration | Owning cloud resource lifecycles at scale |
| **Packer** | Baking machine images once, so servers start already configured | Changes to running fleets |
| **GitOps (Argo CD, Flux)** | Continuously reconciling Kubernetes workloads from Git | Configuring bare VMs |

**Immutable infrastructure** (build an image, replace servers instead of patching them) shrinks the amount of runtime configuration needed. Many teams use Packer and Ansible together: Ansible provisions the image at build time, Terraform deploys it.

> [!pitfall] `shell` and `command` everywhere. They always report `changed` unless you add `creates`, `removes` or `changed_when`, which defeats idempotency and `--check`.
> [!pitfall] Forgetting `become: true` and wondering why package installs fail with permission errors.
> [!pitfall] Variable sprawl. If you cannot say which file defines a variable, the playbook is unmaintainable. Use `defaults/` for overridable values and `group_vars/` per environment.
> [!pitfall] Writing `when: "{{ some_var }}"`. Conditions are already expressions; write `when: some_var`.
> [!pitfall] Unquoted YAML surprises: a file mode like `0644` needs quotes (`"0644"`), and values like `yes`, `no` or `on` can be read as booleans.
> [!pitfall] Running a changed playbook against all of production at once. Use `--check --diff`, then `--limit` to one host, then `serial`.
> [!security] Do not disable SSH host key checking to "make it work". Pre-seed known hosts or use a bastion, and give the automation user only the sudo rules it needs.
> [!security] Third-party roles and collections run as root on your hosts. Pin versions, read what you install, and prefer collections from maintained namespaces.
> [!security] Secrets in plain `group_vars`, in `-e` flags (visible in shell history and process lists) or in logs without `no_log`. Use Vault or a secrets lookup.
> [!tip] Name every task in the imperative ("Install nginx"). The names are your run log and your documentation.
> [!cost] Wall-clock time on big fleets is mostly SSH round trips. Pipelining, fewer small tasks, `gather_facts: false` where possible and more forks are free speedups; a larger control node rarely is.
> [!prod] Run Ansible from CI or AWX with short-lived credentials, keep the inventory and playbooks in Git, and make a scheduled `--check` run your drift detector.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-20 against the ansible-core porting guides: 2.20 requires Python 3.12 or newer on the control node, deprecates `INJECT_FACTS_AS_VARS` (still true by default, flips to false in 2.24) and drops the v2 Galaxy server API; the 2.21 and 2.22 guides were read and list no notable changes (2.22 is in the development docs). The Molecule install notes (default `delegated` driver, drivers in `molecule-plugins`, `ansible-lint` not bundled) come from Molecule's own installation page; the ansible-lint, Molecule and Vault links were found by search, and the `ansible-vault` commands match the Vault guide. NOT verified: Ansible and Molecule are not installed in the sandbox, so the playbooks, role and Molecule scenario were checked only as valid YAML, never run; the `amazon.aws.aws_ec2` inventory plugin options and the collection versions were not checked.
q: What does idempotent mean for an Ansible playbook, and how do you keep command tasks idempotent?
Running it again changes nothing once the host matches the desired state. For command and shell tasks add creates, removes or changed_when so Ansible knows when the work is already done.
How do Terraform and Ansible usually divide the work?
Terraform creates and tracks cloud resources; Ansible configures what runs inside the machines (packages, files, services). Many teams use tags from Terraform to drive a dynamic Ansible inventory.
Why use ansible.builtin.copy instead of copy?
Fully qualified collection names make the module's origin explicit and keep playbooks working when collections change or two collections define the same name.
res: Getting started, modules, playbooks and guides
Python 3.12 requirement, INJECT_FACTS_AS_VARS and Galaxy v2 removal
Behavior changes from 2.20 to 2.21 (none listed as notable)
Testing roles with converge and idempotence checks

iac-at-scale.md:
## Why it exists
The first IaC lesson covered resources, plan and apply on one project. Teams then hit the real problems: a single giant state file that locks everyone, a rename that destroys a database, secrets sitting in state, laptops applying production, and no way to know that someone clicked a console. This lesson covers how to organize and operate IaC safely.

{{dg:0}}

## State is the sharp edge
State maps your code to real resource IDs. Lose it and Terraform wants to recreate everything; corrupt it and plans lie.
- **Remote backend with locking.** On AWS use an S3 bucket with versioning, encryption and public access blocked; recent Terraform and OpenTofu support native S3 lockfile locking (`use_lockfile = true`), replacing the older DynamoDB table. On Azure use a Storage account container; HCP Terraform and similar services also host state.
- **Restrict who can read state.** It can contain secrets in plain text, so treat read access like secret access.
- **Split state to limit blast radius.** One state per environment and per layer (network, data, apps) means a bad apply cannot touch everything and plans stay fast. Wire layers together with outputs and data sources, not copy-pasted IDs.
- **Workspaces are not environments.** CLI workspaces share one backend config and code, which makes it easy to apply to the wrong one. Most teams prefer a directory (or pipeline) per environment calling shared modules.

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10"
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-tfstate-prod"
    key          = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

## Writing code that survives change
- **Modules:** small, single-purpose, versioned (pin `version` or a Git tag), with typed variables, validations and few outputs. Avoid modules that wrap one resource, and deep chains of wrapper modules.
- **`for_each` over `count`** for collections. `count` addresses resources by position, so removing item 2 of 5 shifts the others and destroys and recreates them; `for_each` addresses by key.
- **Refactor without destroying** using declarative blocks, which are reviewable in a pull request, unlike `terraform state mv`:
```hcl
moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.logs
  to   = module.logging.aws_s3_bucket.this
}

import {                      # adopt an existing resource into state
  to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy
  id = "acme-legacy-assets"
}
```
- **Dependencies:** references create implicit ordering; use `depends_on` only for hidden dependencies (for example an IAM policy that must exist before a service starts).
- **Protect critical resources:** `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` on databases and state buckets, plus deletion protection in the cloud resource itself.
- **Multi-region and multi-account:** use provider aliases and an assumed role per target account.

```hcl
variable "buckets" {
  type = map(object({ versioning = bool }))
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "this" {
  for_each = var.buckets
  bucket   = "acme-${each.key}"
}
```

## Testing infrastructure code
1. **Static checks (seconds):** `fmt`, `validate`, `tflint`.
2. **Security and policy scans:** Trivy (which absorbed tfsec) or Checkov flag open security groups, unencrypted storage, and public buckets; OPA or Sentinel enforce organization rules (see policy as code).
3. **Native tests:** `terraform test` and `tofu test` run `.tftest.hcl` files, with `command = plan` for fast assertions or `apply` for real resources and mock providers for no-cost unit tests.
4. **Integration tests:** apply to a throwaway account and assert with Terratest or similar, then destroy.
```hcl
# variables.tf in the module
variable "public" {
  type    = bool
  default = false
  validation {
    condition     = var.public == false
    error_message = "Public buckets are not allowed."
  }
}

# tests/bucket.tftest.hcl
run "rejects_public_buckets" {
  command         = plan
  variables       { public = true }
  expect_failures = [var.public]
}
```

## CI/CD for infrastructure
- Run `plan` on every pull request and post the diff as a comment. Humans review the **plan**, not just the code.
- Apply only from CI on merge, using short-lived credentials from OIDC federation (GitHub Actions to an AWS role or Azure federated credential) instead of long-lived keys. Save the plan file and apply that exact plan.
- Use environment protection or manual approval for production.
- Run a **scheduled plan** (nightly) to detect **drift**: it should be empty; a non-empty plan means someone changed things by hand or an upstream default changed.
- Tools like Atlantis, HCP Terraform, Spacelift and env0 add locking, policy checks and audit trails if you do not want to build this in raw CI.

## Secrets and state encryption
- **Ephemeral resources and write-only arguments** let a secret exist only in memory during an operation and never reach state or plan files. Terraform added ephemeral resources in 1.10 and write-only arguments in 1.11; OpenTofu added both in 1.11 (December 2025). Providers must opt in, so check each resource.
- **State and plan encryption** is native in OpenTofu (since 1.7), with key providers such as AWS KMS, GCP KMS, OpenBao or a passphrase:
```hcl
terraform {
  encryption {
    key_provider "aws_kms" "main" {
      kms_key_id = "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:111122223333:key/example"
      region     = "eu-west-1"
      key_spec   = "AES_256"
    }
    method "aes_gcm" "default" { keys = key_provider.aws_kms.main }
    state { method = method.aes_gcm.default }
    plan  { method = method.aes_gcm.default }
  }
}
```
- Even so, keep secrets in a manager (Secrets Manager, Key Vault) and pass references, not values.

## Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi or CDK?
| Tool | Language | Choose when |
|---|---|---|
| Terraform | HCL | Largest ecosystem and hiring pool; BSL-licensed since 2023 |
| OpenTofu | HCL | You want an open-source (MPL, Linux Foundation) drop-in with built-in state encryption; configs and state diverge once you use OpenTofu-only features |
| Pulumi | TypeScript, Python, Go, C# | You want real loops, functions, unit tests in a general-purpose language |
| AWS CDK / CDKTF-style | General languages | AWS-only shops that like CloudFormation under the hood |

The concepts (state, plan, drift, modules, least privilege) transfer across all of them.

> [!pitfall] Renaming a resource or moving it into a module without a `moved` block. The plan shows destroy and create, and on a database that means data loss. Always read the plan for "must be replaced".
> [!pitfall] `terraform apply -target` as a habit. It skips dependencies and leaves state and code out of step; use it only for emergency recovery.
> [!pitfall] Upgrading a provider major version and applying in the same change. Pin versions, upgrade in a separate pull request, and read the plan.
> [!security] The apply role is a high-value target: it can create IAM and read state. Scope it per environment, require approvals for production, and never let pull requests from forks run apply.
> [!prod] Back up the state bucket (versioning plus cross-region replication) and rehearse recovery. A tested `import` plan is the fallback when state is lost.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-19: OpenTofu 1.11 (December 2025) added ephemeral resources, write-only attributes and the `enabled` meta-argument, and its 1.11.6 patch was current in April 2026 with 1.12 in release candidate. Native S3 lockfile locking and exact version cut-offs were not re-verified in this batch; confirm them in the docs for your version.
q: Why prefer for_each over count for a list of buckets?
count addresses resources by index, so removing one in the middle shifts the rest and forces destroy and recreate. for_each uses stable keys.
What does a moved block give you that terraform state mv does not?
A declarative, reviewable refactor that goes through the pull request and plan, so teammates and CI see it and no one has to run a manual state command.
How do ephemeral resources and write-only arguments reduce secret exposure?
The secret is used in memory during the operation and is never written to the state or plan file, unlike normal attributes.
res: State, modules, moved, import and tests

iac-gitops.md:
## Why it exists
The classic Kubernetes deploy is a CI job that runs `kubectl apply` or `helm upgrade`. It works until it does not: the CI system holds cluster-admin credentials, nobody can say what is *actually* running versus what Git says, a hand-edit with `kubectl edit` silently diverges from the repo, and re-creating a cluster means replaying a pile of pipeline runs.

**GitOps** flips the direction. Git holds the desired state of the cluster. A controller **inside the cluster** pulls that state and continuously reconciles reality toward it. The four OpenGitOps principles are: the system is described **declaratively**; the desired state is **versioned and immutable**; approved changes are **pulled automatically**; and agents **continuously reconcile** drift.

{{dg:0}}

Two benefits follow directly. The cluster credential never leaves the cluster, and every change is a reviewed commit with an author, a diff and an easy revert.

## CI and CD are separate jobs
{{dg:1}}

CI builds, tests and pushes an image (by digest or an immutable tag). A **config repo** change then records "run this image": a pull request, an automated bump by Renovate, Flux image automation or Argo CD Image Updater. The GitOps controller sees the new commit and rolls it out. CI never touches the cluster.

## The two main tools
| | **Argo CD** | **Flux** |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | One application-centric system with a web UI and API | A set of controllers (the GitOps Toolkit) driven by Kubernetes CRDs |
| Main objects | `Application`, `AppProject`, `ApplicationSet` | `GitRepository`, `OCIRepository`, `HelmRepository`, `Kustomization`, `HelmRelease` |
| UI | Rich built-in UI showing the resource tree and diffs | No bundled UI; use CLI, Grafana or third-party and Flux Operator tooling |
| Helm | Renders the chart to manifests and applies them (no Helm release lifecycle) | `helm-controller` runs real Helm releases, with remediation and rollback |
| Multi-cluster | A central instance can manage many registered clusters | Typically one Flux per cluster, all reading one repo |
| Git alternatives | Git, Helm repositories, OCI | Git, OCI artifacts (GA since Flux 2.6), Helm, S3-compatible buckets |
| Ordering | Sync waves and hooks | `dependsOn` between Kustomizations and HelmReleases |
| Both are | CNCF graduated projects, widely used in production | |

Neither is "better". Teams that want a UI, central multi-cluster visibility and ApplicationSets often pick Argo CD; teams that want a lean, Kubernetes-native toolkit with first-class Helm releases and OCI often pick Flux.

## Repo layout that scales
```
platform-config/
  clusters/
    prod/            # what this cluster runs (Argo Applications or Flux Kustomizations)
    staging/
  apps/
    shop-api/
      base/          # deployment.yaml, service.yaml, kustomization.yaml
      overlays/
        staging/     # image tag, replicas, hostnames for staging
        prod/
  infra/             # ingress controller, cert-manager, monitoring
```
Use **directories per environment** (Kustomize overlays or Helm values files), not a long-lived branch per environment. Branch-per-environment turns promotion into painful merges and makes drift between environments invisible. Promotion becomes a pull request that copies a version from `staging` to `prod`.

## Worked example 1: Argo CD
Install (the project's docs use server-side apply because the CRDs are large; check the current instructions):
```bash
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts \
  -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
```

A project is the security boundary: which repos, clusters and namespaces its applications may touch.
```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - https://github.com/acme/platform-config.git
  destinations:
    - server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
      namespace: shop
  clusterResourceWhitelist: []      # no cluster-scoped resources (no CRDs, no ClusterRoles)
```

An application points a path in Git at a namespace in a cluster:
```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: shop-api-prod
  namespace: argocd
  finalizers:
    - resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io
spec:
  project: shop
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/platform-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/shop-api/overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: shop
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true          # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true       # revert manual changes in the cluster
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ServerSideApply=true
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff:
        duration: 10s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 3m
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas   # an HPA owns the replica count; do not fight it
```

An **ApplicationSet** generates many Applications from one template, here one per overlay directory:
```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: shop-envs
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/acme/platform-config.git
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/shop-api/overlays/*
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "shop-api-{{.path.basename}}"
    spec:
      project: shop
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/acme/platform-config.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: "{{.path.path}}"
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "shop-{{.path.basename}}"
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
```
Other generators cover lists of clusters (one app per cluster), pull requests (a preview environment per PR) and matrix combinations.

## Worked example 2: Flux
```bash
flux bootstrap github \
  --owner=acme --repository=platform-config \
  --branch=main --path=clusters/prod --personal=false
```
Bootstrap installs the controllers and commits their own manifests into the repo, so Flux manages itself from Git.

```yaml
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: platform-config
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  url: https://github.com/acme/platform-config
  ref:
    branch: main
---
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: shop-api-prod
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  path: ./apps/shop-api/overlays/prod
  prune: true
  wait: true              # report Ready only when resources are healthy
  timeout: 5m
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: platform-config
  dependsOn:
    - name: infra-controllers
```
A real Helm release, with automatic remediation:
```yaml
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: ingress-nginx
  namespace: ingress-nginx
spec:
  interval: 1h
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: ingress-nginx
      version: ">=4.11.0 <5.0.0"
      sourceRef:
        kind: HelmRepository
        name: ingress-nginx
        namespace: flux-system
  install:
    remediation:
      retries: 3
  upgrade:
    remediation:
      retries: 3
  values:
    controller:
      replicaCount: 2
```
Useful commands: `flux get kustomizations`, `flux reconcile kustomization shop-api-prod --with-source`, `flux diff kustomization shop-api-prod --path ./apps/shop-api/overlays/prod`, and for Argo CD `argocd app diff shop-api-prod` and `argocd app sync shop-api-prod`.

## Ordering, health and hooks
- **Argo CD sync waves:** annotate resources with `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "-1"` (lower waves go first and must be healthy before the next wave). **Hooks** (`argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync`) run a Job, for example a database migration, before the main sync.
- **Flux:** use `dependsOn` so CRDs and controllers are installed and ready before the resources that use them, and `wait: true` plus health checks to gate readiness.
- **App of apps:** a parent Application whose manifests are themselves Applications. It bootstraps a whole cluster from one root. ApplicationSets are usually the more maintainable way to generate many similar apps.

## Secrets in a Git-driven world
You must never commit a plain Kubernetes `Secret` (base64 is not encryption). Three standard answers:

| Approach | How it works | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|
| **Sealed Secrets** | Encrypt with the cluster's public key; a controller decrypts into a `Secret` | Simple; ciphertext is bound to one cluster's key, so back that key up |
| **SOPS** (with age, AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault or GCP KMS) | Encrypt values inside YAML files in Git; the controller decrypts at apply time | Flux supports it natively; Argo CD needs a plugin or tool such as KSOPS |
| **External Secrets Operator** | Git holds an `ExternalSecret` that *references* a secret in AWS Secrets Manager, Key Vault, Vault and so on; the operator creates the Kubernetes `Secret` | Secret values never enter Git; you depend on the external store |

A SOPS setup for Flux:
```yaml
# .sops.yaml
creation_rules:
  - path_regex: .*\.enc\.yaml$
    encrypted_regex: ^(data|stringData)$
    age: age1examplepublickeyreplacewithyourown
```
```yaml
# on the Flux Kustomization
spec:
  decryption:
    provider: sops
    secretRef:
      name: sops-age
```
Keep the private key out of Git, back it up, and rotate it with a plan.

## Progressive delivery
GitOps decides *what* should run; progressive delivery controls *how fast* it rolls out. **Argo Rollouts** adds a `Rollout` resource with canary and blue-green strategies and automated analysis; **Flagger** does similar work in the Flux ecosystem.

```yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: shop-api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: shop-api
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: shop-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/shop-api@sha256:0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef
```
Without a service mesh or a supported ingress, weights are approximated by replica ratios; with one, traffic is split precisely. Add an analysis step that queries your metrics and aborts the rollout on a bad error rate.

## Operating it
| Topic | Practice |
|---|---|
| **Drift** | `selfHeal` (Argo) or periodic reconcile (Flux) reverts manual changes; alert when something stays out of sync |
| **Access** | Humans change the cluster through pull requests; keep a documented, audited break-glass path |
| **Blast radius** | A central Argo CD with credentials to many clusters is a high-value target; use projects, per-cluster scoping and network controls |
| **Promotion** | A pull request that changes the version in the next environment's overlay, with automated checks |
| **Previews** | Argo ApplicationSet pull-request generator, or Flux with per-PR Kustomizations, for ephemeral environments |
| **Scale** | Argo CD repo-server rendering and Git polling can bottleneck: use webhooks, shard, and avoid giant monolithic paths |
| **Upgrades** | Both projects release often; read release notes and test upgrades in a non-production cluster first |

> [!pitfall] `selfHeal` fighting something else that legitimately edits the object: an HPA changing replicas, a mutating webhook injecting sidecars, an operator updating status fields. Use `ignoreDifferences` (Argo) or adjust the owner of those fields.
> [!pitfall] `prune: true` pointed at the wrong path can delete live resources. Start with prune off, review the diff, and use AppProject boundaries.
> [!pitfall] Mutable image tags such as `latest`. The manifest never changes, so the controller sees no diff and nothing rolls out. Use immutable tags or digests.
> [!pitfall] Branch-per-environment. Promotions become merge conflicts and environments drift apart without anyone noticing.
> [!pitfall] Installing a CRD and a resource that uses it in the same unordered sync. Order them with waves or `dependsOn`.
> [!pitfall] Deleting a parent app-of-apps with cascading finalizers set and removing every child's workloads with it. Know what your finalizers do before you delete.
> [!security] The GitOps controller is effectively cluster-admin, so write access to the config repo is write access to the cluster. Use branch protection, required reviews, CODEOWNERS and signed commits (Flux can verify commit and tag signatures), and scope Argo AppProjects tightly. Keep the controllers patched; both have had security advisories.
> [!security] Plaintext Secrets in Git stay in history forever, even after deletion. Rotate anything that leaked and use one of the secret patterns above.
> [!tip] Run `kustomize build` or `helm template` and a manifest linter and policy check in CI on every pull request, so a bad manifest never reaches the controller. `flux diff` and `argocd app diff` preview the cluster impact.
> [!cost] Rendering large Helm charts or Kustomize trees on every poll costs controller CPU and memory. Prefer webhooks over short polling intervals, split huge paths, and cache.
> [!prod] Treat the GitOps controller as production infrastructure: run it highly available, monitor sync failures and out-of-sync duration, and keep a tested procedure to rebuild a cluster from the repo.
> [!version] Verified 2026-10-20 by web search. Argo CD: the install command (`kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side --force-conflicts -f .../stable/manifests/install.yaml`) matches the official Getting Started page, which explains that server-side apply is needed because some CRDs exceed the client-side annotation size limit; the project's GitHub release pages show the 3.5.x line (3.5.5 was the newest seen, and 3.5.4 carried coordinated security fixes), so pin a version rather than tracking `stable`. A third-party report (one measurement, not reproduced) says an app-of-apps wave on 3.5.3 could start while a child with a failed resource read Healthy, so test your own wave gates. Flux: the 2.9 GA announcement is dated 2026-06-30 (CLI plugin system, server-side apply field ignore rules, Age post-quantum SOPS decryption, Helm post-render strategies, OIDC receivers); OCI artifacts went GA in 2.6, image automation GA and `source-watcher` came in 2.7, and `flux migrate` is needed when upgrading from older versions to 2.7 or later. The YAML uses `source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1`, `kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1` and `helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2`, the versions shown in current Flux docs. NOT verified: no Kubernetes cluster was available, so the Argo CD, Argo Rollouts, Flux and SOPS YAML was only parsed, never applied; the External Secrets Operator apiVersion is still left out on purpose; the Cosign v3 claim for Flux 2.8 was not re-checked.
q: Why does a pull-based GitOps controller improve security over a CI job that runs kubectl apply?
The cluster credential stays inside the cluster; CI only needs to write to Git. Every change is a reviewed commit, and the controller keeps reconciling, so out-of-band edits are detected or reverted.
Why is a long-lived branch per environment a poor promotion strategy?
Promotion becomes merge conflicts, and environments silently drift apart. Directories or overlays per environment make promotion an explicit pull request that copies a version.
Name three ways to keep Secrets out of Git in a GitOps setup.
Sealed Secrets (encrypt to a cluster key), SOPS (encrypt values in files, decrypted by the controller), and External Secrets Operator (Git holds a reference; values live in a secrets manager).

iac-terraform.md:
## Why it exists
Clicking through a cloud console works for one server and fails for fifty. Nobody remembers which checkbox was ticked, staging quietly differs from production, and recreating an environment after a disaster takes days. **Infrastructure as code (IaC)** moves infrastructure into text files that live in Git: reviewed in pull requests, versioned, repeatable and testable.

**Terraform** (HashiCorp, now owned by IBM) is the most widely used IaC tool. It is **declarative**: you describe the end state ("one S3 bucket with versioning, one database in this subnet") and Terraform works out the steps. **OpenTofu** is the open-source fork under the Linux Foundation, created after Terraform moved to the Business Source License in August 2023. The language (HCL), the workflow and the provider ecosystem are shared, so almost everything here applies to both. This lesson writes `terraform`; replace it with `tofu` for OpenTofu.

{{dg:0}}

Mental model: three things must agree. **Code** is what you want, **state** is what Terraform believes exists, and the **real cloud** is what actually exists. `plan` compares all three and `apply` closes the gap.

## How it works
- **Providers** are plugins that translate resources into API calls (`hashicorp/aws`, `hashicorp/azurerm`, Cloudflare, GitHub, Supabase, even Kubernetes). They are downloaded by `terraform init` and pinned in `.terraform.lock.hcl`, which you commit.
- **Resources** are things to manage (`aws_s3_bucket`). **Data sources** read things that already exist. **Variables** are inputs, **outputs** are results, **locals** are named expressions.
- **State** is a JSON mapping from your resource addresses to real IDs plus their last known attributes. It is how Terraform knows that `aws_s3_bucket.assets` is bucket `acme-assets-prod`. Lose it and Terraform wants to create everything again.
- **Remote backend and locking.** Teams store state in shared storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS, HCP Terraform) so only one `apply` runs at a time. Since Terraform 1.10 and OpenTofu 1.10 the S3 backend can lock with a lock file in the bucket (`use_lockfile = true`), so the old DynamoDB lock table is no longer needed.
- **Modules** are reusable folders of resources with inputs and outputs. A **root module** is the folder you run commands in; one root module usually equals one state file.
- **Graph.** Terraform builds a dependency graph from references (`aws_s3_bucket.assets.id`), creates independent resources in parallel and destroys in reverse order.

## Worked example
A versioned, private bucket with a validated variable, remote state and an output.

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.10"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0" # pin the major version your team has tested
    }
  }
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "acme-tfstate-prod"
    key          = "assets/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

variable "env" {
  type        = string
  description = "Deployment environment"
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.env)
    error_message = "env must be dev, staging or prod."
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "acme-assets-${var.env}"
  tags   = { Environment = var.env, ManagedBy = "terraform" }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "assets" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "assets" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.assets.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

output "assets_bucket_arn" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.assets.arn
}
```

Day-to-day commands:

```bash
terraform init                       # download providers, configure backend
terraform fmt -recursive             # canonical formatting
terraform validate                   # syntax and type check, no cloud calls
terraform plan -var env=staging -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan               # applies exactly what was planned
terraform state list                 # what is Terraform tracking?
terraform destroy -var env=dev       # tear down a throwaway environment
```

Repeating a resource per item with `for_each`, and reusing a module:

```hcl
variable "buckets" {
  type    = set(string)
  default = ["uploads", "exports", "backups"]
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "app" {
  for_each = var.buckets
  bucket   = "acme-${each.key}-${var.env}"
}

module "network" {
  source  = "./modules/network"   # or a registry module with a pinned version
  cidr    = "10.20.0.0/16"
  env     = var.env
}
```

Bringing existing resources under management and renaming safely (no console clicking, no state surgery):

```hcl
import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.legacy
  id = "acme-legacy-bucket"
}

moved {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.assets
  to   = aws_s3_bucket.assets_v2
}
```

## In real products
- **Pull request workflow.** CI runs `fmt`, `validate` and `plan` on every PR and posts the plan as a comment; `apply` runs only after merge to main. Tools that do this: Atlantis, HCP Terraform, Spacelift, env0, GitHub Actions or GitLab CI with your own scripts.
- **No long-lived cloud keys in CI.** Use OIDC federation: the pipeline gets a short-lived token and assumes a role (AWS IAM role, Azure federated credential). See the Git/CI/CD and OAuth lessons.
- **Layering.** Split state by blast radius and change rate: `network`, `data`, `app` per environment, not one giant root module (the "terralith"). Pass values between layers with outputs or data sources.
- **Policy as code.** OPA/Conftest, Sentinel, Checkov, tfsec/Trivy scan the plan JSON and block things like public buckets or open security groups before apply.
- **Drift detection.** A scheduled `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` (exit code 2 means changes) catches manual console edits.
- **GitOps for Kubernetes** (Argo CD, Flux) applies the same idea inside the cluster: Git is the source of truth and a controller reconciles.

## Trade-offs
| Option | Strength | Weakness | Pick it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Terraform | Biggest ecosystem, most modules and examples, HCP Terraform and Sentinel | BSL license, IBM-controlled roadmap | You want the incumbent and vendor support |
| OpenTofu | MPL license, Linux Foundation, drop-in for most code, state encryption | Smaller vendor tooling; features can diverge | New projects, license concerns, open-source requirements |
| Pulumi / AWS CDK | Real languages (TypeScript, Python), loops and tests feel natural | Easier to write unreadable infrastructure; smaller review culture | App developers own infrastructure |
| CloudFormation / Bicep | First-party, no external state to manage | One cloud each; CloudFormation errors are verbose | You are all-in on one cloud |

> [!pitfall] State holds secrets in plain text. Database passwords and keys that pass through resources end up in `terraform.tfstate`. Use an encrypted remote backend, restrict who can read it, never commit state, and prefer ephemeral resources and write-only arguments (Terraform 1.10 and 1.11) or a secrets manager reference for sensitive values.
> [!pitfall] Reading a plan lazily. `-/+` means destroy and recreate; on a database that is data loss. Look for replacements before approving, and add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to stateful resources.
> [!pitfall] Manual console edits create drift. The next apply silently reverts them (or fails). Make the console read-only for managed resources.
> [!security] Give the plan job a read-only role and the apply job a separate, narrower-in-time role gated by environment approval. A plan that can write is an apply you did not review.
> [!tip] Pin provider and module versions, commit the lock file, and upgrade in a dedicated PR. `terraform init -upgrade` plus a reviewed plan is a normal change.
> [!cost] Running `terraform destroy` on dev environments overnight is one of the cheapest savings you can automate. Tag everything so cost reports map back to code.
> [!prod] Versions move quickly. As of mid-2026 OpenTofu 1.12 shipped (May 2026) and Terraform was on the 1.15 line, with 1.16 reported for August 2026. Verified 2026-10-17 from secondary sources, not official release pages. Pin exact versions in CI and read the upgrade notes before bumping.
q: What are the three things Terraform reconciles, and which command shows the difference?
Your code (desired state), the state file (what Terraform believes exists) and the real cloud. `terraform plan` shows the diff; `apply` executes it.
Why must state be stored remotely and locked for a team?
Two people applying at once can corrupt state or create duplicate resources. A shared backend gives one source of truth, and locking (S3 `use_lockfile`, Blob leases, HCP Terraform) serializes runs.
A plan shows `-/+` on your production database. What does it mean and what do you do?

The resource will be destroyed and recreated, losing data. Stop, find which argument forces replacement, change it in place if possible or plan a migration, and protect stateful resources with `prevent_destroy`.
How is OpenTofu different from Terraform in practice?

Same HCL and workflow, but OpenTofu is MPL-licensed under the Linux Foundation and adds features like state encryption; Terraform is BSL-licensed under IBM and has HCP Terraform and Sentinel. Most code runs unchanged on either.
Why use OIDC for CI instead of storing cloud access keys as secrets?
OIDC gives the pipeline short-lived credentials for a specific role per run, so there is nothing long-lived to leak, and trust can be limited to one repository and branch.
